statement: London has taken a holiday from wickedness, and nothing in the street below requires the smallest explanation.
The opera glass is French, bought for the opera and used for everything else; the eye is the instrument, and the glass merely brings the street nearer.
The pale sandy dust of the Heath road, white to the ankle, is what four miles of walking in from Hampstead presses into a boot; that is why Holmes named Hampstead and not merely somewhere north.

The victualler's coat is good cloth kept rather than replaced, a tradesman's economy; the girl beside him walks with a daughter's easy step, and keeps glancing at the clock over the chemist's, as a daughter does who was due home an hour ago.
The dust on a boot is observed, and Watson could have named it himself; that the man walked from Hampstead is inferred, and wants practice before it wants confidence.
Two readings, both correct: Holmes will not touch the violin before midnight; one wrong, and Watson reads the monograph on tobacco ash, plates and all.
Holmes has been at the violin on and off since Saturday; if Watson wins he will not touch it before midnight, and he keeps his word.
The monograph upon the ashes of the various tobaccos describes a hundred and forty varieties, with coloured plates.
The old man by the cab rank is waiting for a grandchild: he watches the crowd at the height of a child's head, not a man's.

statement: The clergyman is an actor in costume, greasepaint at his hairline and a script in his hand, between the matinée and the evening performance at a West End house, in a melodrama with a clergyman in it, not wanted until the second act.
Holmes knew Watson for a man back from Afghanistan the day they met, seven years ago: he had served with his regiment in India, and been sent home from the base hospital at Peshawar.
We see what asks to be seen.
